When a machine breaks down

Machines break. Hydraulic hoses burst, tracks throw, engines overheat in May.

A dedicated mechanical support team keeps the network’s machines running, so that a burst hose is an inconvenience and never a project delay. When a repair will take longer than the job can wait, the network supplies another machine of the same class. That is how an uptime commitment of 98% is kept. Not by machines that never fail, but by a replacement that is a short drive away.

Classes, and what each is for

Excavators are named by their working weight. The weight tells you the bucket, the reach and, in this district, whether the machine will make any impression on the ground at all.

Small, 5 to 8 tonnes
Works inside buildings, between pipe racks and under conveyors. Opens cable trenches and drains beside live plant, where a larger machine would be a danger to everything around it.
Medium, 13 to 22 tonnes
The daily machine. Foundations, drains, loading tippers, lowering pipes into a trench. The 20-tonne class carries a bucket of about one cubic metre.
Heavy, 30 to 35 tonnes
Bulk excavation, hard digging, and a breaker large enough for weathered rock and jointed basalt.
Very heavy, 45 to 50 tonnes
For sound basalt. This class carries the heaviest breakers, and it is the reason our network was built the way it was.

Typical figures

Bucket sizes and reach differ from one maker to the next, and the machine’s own chart governs. Tell us the job and we will match the class to it.

What decides the class

  • The ground. Soil, soft limestone, marl, weathered rock or basalt. See The ground beneath us.
  • Depth and reach. How deep, and how far from where the machine can stand.
  • Room. Headroom under a gallery, tail swing beside a wall, the width of a gate.
  • What it loads into. The height of the tipper’s body.
  • What it must not touch. Cables, pipes and the foundations of running machines.
  • How it gets there. A 50-tonne machine comes on a low-loader, after a route survey.

Attachments

Digging bucket
General excavation.
Rock bucket
Thicker, narrower, with heavier teeth, for broken rock.
Trenching bucket
Narrow, for cable and pipe trenches.
Rock breaker
A hydraulic hammer in place of the bucket. See Rock breakers.
Lifting point
An excavator may lift a pipe or a manhole ring only from a rated lifting point, within its chart, with the area clear. A bucket tooth is not a hook.

Digging beside a running plant

  1. Read the drawings and walk the ground

    Buried cables and pipes are marked from the plant’s drawings and from a scan. Where there is doubt, trial pits are dug by hand.

  2. Take the excavation permit

    Signed by each plant department whose services lie below.

  3. Set the swing zone

    The radius of the arm and of the tail is barricaded. One banksman, one set of signals.

  4. Dig to line and level

    The last layer above founding level is trimmed with care, so that the ground is not loosened below the foundation it will carry.

  5. Keep the edge safe

    Spoil and machines stay back from the edge. Deep cuts are sloped, benched or supported. Every pit gets a ladder and a hard barricade.

  6. Offer the bottom for inspection

    Before anything covers it.

What we watch for

An unmarked cable
Hand-dug trial pits and a scan come first. Digging stops at the first warning tape or tile.
Overhead lines and galleries
The reach of the boom is checked against everything above it before the machine is positioned.
People in the swing
A barricade, a banksman, and an operator who stops the moment anyone steps inside.
Undermining a neighbour
Excavation beside an existing foundation is taken down in short lengths, in the sequence the engineer sets.
Water
Near the shore the pit will make water. Sumps and pumps are part of the plan, not an afterthought.

Ask for it this way

“One 20-tonne excavator with bucket, a single shift a day for three weeks, at the limestone crusher, from Monday. The ground is weathered rock below one metre.”

That is enough for us to answer the same day.

Why a hammer and not a blast

Inside a working plant, blasting is rarely welcome. It throws rock, shakes foundations and stops everything within reach while the area is cleared. A breaker works a few metres from a running conveyor, at any hour, and needs nothing but a permit and a barricade.

AspectBlastingBreaking
PermissionsExplosives licence, magazine, blaster, noticesAn excavation permit
Effect on the plantArea cleared, work nearby stopped for each blastWork continues around a barricaded zone
VibrationA sharp shock, controlled by charge and delayContinuous and local, monitored where it matters
Shape of the cutRough. Overbreak is common.Close to line and level
Best forLarge volumes in open groundRock beside structures, services and running plant

Where the volume is large and the ground is open, a blast may still be the right answer, and we say so.

A hammer matched to its carrier

A breaker is chosen for the excavator that carries it. Too small, and the job crawls. Too large, and it shakes the boom to pieces. The heavier the carrier, the harder the blow, which is why sound basalt calls for the 45 to 50 tonne class.

Moil point
A pointed tool. The general choice for hard, massive rock.
Chisel
A flat edge. For bedded or jointed rock, and for trimming a trench to line.
Blunt
A flat face. For breaking boulders that are already loose.

How a good operator reads rock

Basalt cooled from lava, and as it cooled it cracked into columns and blocks. Those joints are the operator’s allies.

  1. Find a free face

    Rock breaks towards open space. The work begins at an edge and moves inward, a step at a time.

  2. Set the tool square

    The tool is placed at right angles to the rock and pressed down before the hammer fires.

  3. Thirty seconds, then move

    If the rock has not cracked in half a minute, the point is in the wrong place. Staying longer only heats the tool.

  4. Never fire into air

    When the rock gives way the hammer stops. Blank blows destroy the breaker from the inside.

  5. Never lever

    The tool is a hammer, not a crowbar. Prising with it snaps it.

At founding level

The last few hundred millimetres above a foundation are the ones that matter. A heavy breaker driven carelessly to the bottom shatters the rock that was meant to carry the load.

So the final layer is taken with a lighter hammer and then by hand. The surface is cleaned with compressed air and water, and offered to the engineer before blinding concrete covers it.

What we watch for

Flying chips
An exclusion zone around the machine, a guard on the cab, and eye protection for anyone who must be near.
Noise
Hearing protection inside the zone. Night working near a township is agreed with the plant first.
Dust
Water spray at the point of breaking.
Vibration
Beside a running machine, fresh concrete or an old structure, we agree limits with the plant and monitor them. A saw cut or a line of drilled holes can separate the work from what must not be shaken.
Wear
The tool is greased every couple of hours of hammering. A dry tool seizes.

Breaker hours are recorded apart from bucket hours on the machine’s log, because a hammer wears a machine differently. See How hire works.

What a dozer is for

Clearing
Scrub, topsoil and rubble stripped from a site before anything else begins.
Spreading
Fill tipped by lorries is pushed out in even layers, ready for the roller.
Rough grading
Platforms, yards and road formations shaped to within a hand’s width of level.
Stockpiles
Limestone, coal, gypsum and clinker heaps trimmed, pushed up and kept in shape.
Ripping
A tooth at the rear tears up weathered rock and hard crust so that an excavator can load it.
Haul roads
Ruts filled and surfaces kept true through the monsoon.
Recovery
When a loaded tipper sinks to its axles in July, the dozer is what brings it out.

Where it is the wrong machine

  • Long distances. Pushing earth much beyond a hundred metres wastes fuel and time. An excavator and tippers do it better.
  • Fine levels. A dozer shapes ground. It does not finish it.
  • Sound rock. That is work for a breaker.

How we work one

  1. Agree the levels

    Pegs and a reference level are set by the surveyor before the blade drops. A dozer can move a great deal of earth to the wrong height very quickly.

  2. Push downhill where possible

    The machine and gravity work together. Material is moved in the direction the ground already falls.

  3. Spread in layers

    Fill goes down in layers thin enough for the roller to compact. A thick layer rolled hard is still loose underneath.

  4. Keep off the edge

    At a tip face or an embankment, a bund of earth is left along the edge and a spotter stands where the operator can see them.

  5. Water the dust

    A tanker follows the work in the dry months.

On a stockpile

A heap of limestone or coal looks solid. Above a reclaim tunnel it may not be.

Draw points

Material drawn from below can leave a hollow under a crust that looks sound. A dozer does not cross a draw point while the feeder beneath it is running, and the operator is told where every draw point is before the shift begins.

On coal, a dozer also compacts the heap, which slows the air that feeds spontaneous heating. The plant’s stockyard rules govern, and our operators are inducted in them.

Ask for it this way

“One bulldozer with ripper, a month, double shift, for spreading fill at the new stockyard. Fill arrives by tipper from six in the morning.”

Reading the number

Every crane carries a load chart. It lists what the crane may lift at each length of boom and each distance from its centre. The headline figure sits in the first corner of that chart: shortest boom, smallest radius, firm level ground, outriggers fully out.

Move the load three times as far out, and the same crane may lift only a quarter of it.

So the question is never “what size of crane?” It is always “how heavy, how far out and how high?” The chart answers the rest.

Two kinds

Truck-mounted cranes

A telescopic boom on a road-going carrier. It drives to the job, sets its outriggers and lifts from one spot. This is the crane for a planned lift: a fan casing, a motor, a length of gallery. Our network reaches the 35-tonne class.

Pick-and-carry cranes

The yellow crane every Indian plant knows as a Hydra. It lifts a load and travels with it, which makes it the daily workhorse for shifting material across a yard. Some plants no longer permit the older articulated type and ask for the newer design with the cabin in front. We send what your rule allows.

What every lift needs

  1. A known weight

    From the drawing, the name plate or a weighbridge. The hook block, slings and shackles are added to it. A guessed weight is the commonest cause of a crane on its side.

  2. A measured radius

    From the centre of the crane to the centre of the load, where the load will be at its farthest. Measured with a tape, not by eye.

  3. The chart

    Read for that boom length and that radius. We plan ordinary lifts well inside the chart.

  4. Firm ground

    Outriggers fully extended, on pads or mats. Never over a covered drain, a cable trench or fresh fill.

  5. Clear air

    Overhead lines, galleries and pipe racks are checked against the boom’s whole path. Near power lines the plant sets the clearance, and the line is isolated where the lift demands it.

  6. Sound tackle

    Slings, shackles and hooks carry their identification and their test certificate, and are looked over before each use.

  7. One signaller

    One person gives signals. The operator obeys a stop from anyone.

  8. A trial

    The load is raised a hand’s width and held. If it hangs level and nothing creeps, the lift goes on.

Routine and critical

Most lifts are routine. Some are not, and those are planned on paper and reviewed by our engineering panel before the crane is booked.

A lift is treated as critical when it uses most of the crane’s capacity at that radius, when two cranes share one load, when the load passes over running plant or occupied buildings, or when the piece is irreplaceable.

Travelling with a load

A pick-and-carry crane is at its most dangerous when it is moving.

  • The load is carried low, close in and tied against swing.
  • The route is walked first. It must be firm and level. A side slope that a car would not notice can put a loaded crane over.
  • Speed is walking pace, and a signaller walks with it, to one side.
  • Nobody rides on the crane or the load.

What it does that others cannot

Height
A lattice boom can be built long enough to reach the top of tall steel.
Radius
It holds a useful load far from its centre, where a telescopic crane has little left.
Travel
On level, prepared ground it can walk with a load on the hook.
Staying power
It stands on a site for the whole season of erection and lifts every day.

What it asks in return

A crawler crane is not hired casually.

Room to be built
The boom is assembled flat on the ground, section by section. That needs a clear strip as long as the boom itself.
Ground that will carry it
All the weight of crane and load goes down through two tracks. The bearing pressure is calculated and the ground is prepared, usually with timber or steel mats.
A way in
Boom sections, counterweights and the base machine arrive on separate trailers. The route and the gate are surveyed first.
Time
Rigging takes days, not hours, and usually a second crane to assist.
Weather
A long boom is a sail. Wind limits are lower than people expect, and they are obeyed.

How a heavy lift is planned

  1. Weights from drawings

    Every piece, with its rigging. Where a drawing is doubtful, the piece is weighed.

  2. The crane’s configuration

    Boom length, counterweight and radius are chosen from the chart for the heaviest and the farthest lift, not the average one.

  3. The standing

    Where the crane sits for each lift, and the path between standings. Ground bearing is checked at every one.

  4. The sequence

    Which piece goes first, where each waits, and how the structure stays stable while it is incomplete.

  5. The exclusion zone

    Drawn on a plan, fenced on the ground, and agreed with every other contractor working nearby.

  6. The weather watch

    A named person decides, before each lift, whether the wind allows it.

The plan is written by people who have rigged before and is reviewed by our engineering panel. On the day, one lift supervisor is in charge, and nobody else gives orders to the crane.

Before you ask for one

Tell us four things: the heaviest piece, how high it must go, how far from where a crane could stand, and for how many weeks. We will tell you which crane the lift needs. If that class is working elsewhere in the network, we will tell you when it is free, or arrange one from farther afield and say so.

We will not send a smaller crane because it happens to be available. A crane that is nearly big enough is the most expensive machine on any site.

The rigs in our network are hydraulic rotary rigs. A mast stands upright on a tracked base. Down the mast hangs a telescopic steel bar called a kelly, and on the end of the kelly turns the drilling tool.

A spiral that screws into soil and brings it up on its flights.

A cylinder with a hinged bottom, for wet or loose ground that would fall off an auger.

Heavier augers and core barrels with hard teeth, for the socket into rock.
Casing
A steel tube that lines the top of the bore and stops it collapsing.

How a bored pile is made, from setting out to testing, is described on Piles, pile caps and rafts. This page is about what the rig needs.

A rig alone bores holes. A piling operation needs rather more.

  • A service crane, or the rig’s own winch, to lower cages and tremie pipes
  • Tremie pipes and a hopper
  • Casing, and the means to install and withdraw it

Firm, level and wide enough for the rig to track and turn. When a rig goes over, it is nearly always because of the ground under one track.

The mast is tall. Overhead lines and galleries decide where a rig can and cannot stand.
Access
The rig travels on a low-loader with its mast folded. Gates, bends and bridges are checked.

Piles are bored in an order that never puts the rig beside concrete that is only hours old.

    Set up

    The rig is positioned over the pile mark. The mast is plumbed, and the position is checked again by the surveyor.

    Bore

    Tool down, turn, lift, spoil off. The depth is logged, and so is each change of stratum.

  3. Midday

What a roller does

Loose fill is full of air. Under load, the air is squeezed out and the ground goes down, taking the road or the floor with it. A roller squeezes the air out first, so that the settlement happens before anything is built.

A vibratory roller does this with a heavy steel drum that shakes as it rolls. The vibration lets the particles slide past one another into a tighter packing than dead weight alone would achieve.

Smooth drum
For sand, gravel, crushed stone and road base.
Padfoot drum
A drum with raised feet that knead clay and silty soil.
Hand-guided compactors
For trenches, edges and the strip beside a wall where a roller cannot go.

The three things that decide the result

  1. Layer thickness

    Fill is spread in thin layers and each is compacted before the next goes down. A thick layer rolled twenty times is tight on top and loose below.

  2. Moisture

    Every soil has a moisture content at which it compacts best. Too dry and the particles will not slide. Too wet and the water holds them apart. In May a water tanker works ahead of the roller. In July the work waits for the ground to dry.

  3. Passes

    How many times the roller goes over. Not a matter of opinion. It is found on a trial strip at the start of the job.

Proving it

Compaction is measured, not judged by the look of the surface.

A laboratory finds the greatest density that the soil can reach. In the field, the density actually achieved is tested layer by layer and compared with it. The specification sets the pass mark, commonly 95 to 98 per cent of the laboratory figure.

A layer that fails is watered or dried, rolled again and tested again. The next layer does not go down on a failure.

What we watch for

Edges
The edge of an embankment is the least compacted part. It is built wide and trimmed back.
Beside structures
No heavy vibration near green concrete, old walls or buried pipes. Smaller machines, more passes.
A surface that rocks
If the ground moves like a mattress under the drum, it is too wet or there is a soft spot below. It is dug out and replaced, not rolled harder.
Rain
An unsealed layer left open to rain is lost. The surface is rolled smooth and given a fall before the crew leaves.
Slopes
A roller works up and down a slope, never across it.

“One vibratory roller, smooth drum, with operator, for six weeks. Granular sub-base for an internal road, layers tested by the plant’s laboratory.”

The transit mixer

A steel drum on a lorry, with spiral blades inside. Turning one way, the blades fold the concrete back into the drum and keep it mixed. Turning the other way, they screw it out of the chute.

A typical drum carries about six cubic metres. On the road it turns slowly, a few times a minute, just enough to stop the stone settling out of the paste.

The clock

From the moment of batching, a clock runs. The Indian standard for ready-mixed concrete, IS 4926, expects a load to be discharged within about two hours. In the heat of May the real margin is shorter, unless the mix was designed with a retarder for the journey.

So the route, the gate, the weighbridge queue and the place where a mixer waits its turn are all planned before the first load is batched.

The one thing a driver may never do

Water added at the pour to loosen a stiff load buys an easy afternoon and a weak structure. No water is added to a mixer at site. If a load has stiffened beyond use, it is rejected.

A drum is washed after every load. The wash water is strongly alkaline and full of cement fines. It goes to a lined washout pit agreed with the plant. It does not go into a stormwater drain.

Two kinds

Line pumps

A pump on a trailer, pushing concrete through a steel pipeline laid to the pour. The line can run a long way along the ground, into a building, or up the side of a structure. This is how concrete reaches a silo roof or a floor high in a preheater tower.

Boom pumps

A pump on a lorry with a folding, jointed boom that carries the pipeline through the air. It sets up in minutes and places concrete anywhere within its reach. This is the machine for rafts, slabs and large foundations.

What a pump needs from the mix

A pump moves concrete as a plug, sliding on a thin film of cement paste against the pipe wall. If the paste is too thin or too scarce, the stones lock together and the line blocks.

  • A cohesive mix that does not bleed or segregate
  • Workable, but not sloppy
  • A well-graded blend with enough fine material
  • Stone no larger than the line can pass, usually 20 mm
  • A steady supply. A pump that waits in hot weather is a pump that blocks.

The mix is designed as a pumped mix from the start. A pour is not the place to find out.

Setting up

  1. Stand it properly

    Outriggers out, on pads, on ground that will carry them. Not beside an open excavation.

  2. Look up

    A boom and a power line must never be near each other. The clearance is the plant’s rule, and it is generous.

  3. Lay and anchor the line

    Every bend pushes back when the pump strokes. Bends are anchored. A vertical riser is clamped to the structure, not hung from it.

  4. Prime

    A cement grout goes through first to coat the pipe. It is caught and discarded, not placed in the structure.

  5. Keep it moving

    In heat, concrete is not left standing in the line. If the next mixer is late, the pump strokes slowly to keep the plug alive.

  6. Clean out

    A sponge ball is driven through with water. The washings go to the washout pit.

When a line blocks

The pressure rises and the line jerks. The operator reverses a few strokes to relieve it and tries again.

Stored pressure

A blocked line holds pressure like a spring. No coupling is opened until the pump has been reversed and the pressure released, and then only by the pump crew, standing to one side.

After any blockage, and at every start, nobody holds the end hose. Trapped air can whip it with enough force to kill.

On a large pour

  • A second pump stands by, primed, with its own line where the pour cannot be allowed to stop.
  • The pump operator and the pour supervisor are in direct contact, by radio where they cannot see each other.
  • The boom is never swung over people.
  • At night the whole standing, the hopper and the end of the line are lit.

Ask for it this way

“One boom pump for a raft of 450 m³, pour to start at eight in the evening. Reach needed, about 30 metres from the road. Standby pump required.”

How a route is built

  1. Start from where people live

    Townships, Rajula, Jafrabad and the villages between. We map who needs to travel, from where, for which shift.

  2. Draw the routes

    So that no one rides much longer than they must and no bus runs half empty. The shift bus planner shows the arithmetic.

  3. Fix the stops and the minutes

    Every stop has a time. The bus keeps it, so that nobody stands on a dark road wondering.

  4. Size the vehicles

    A bus where the numbers justify one. A mini-bus for the thinner routes.

  5. Keep a spare

    Behind every route there is a vehicle and a driver who can cover it.

What the plant can expect

Punctuality
Arrival at the gate before shift change, with time to walk in. Recorded daily.
A replacement
If a bus fails, another is sent. The route is not cancelled.
Safe drivers
Licensed for passenger vehicles, medically fit, rested, and known to us.
Sound vehicles
Papers current. Tyres, brakes, lights and emergency exit checked.
A seat for everyone
No standing passengers on a highway route.
Night routes
Planned with care for where each person is set down, and in what order.
One number
A coordinator who can be reached when a bus is late, by the plant and by the passengers.

Shutdowns and peaks

When a shutdown brings several hundred extra people to the gate, the fleet grows to carry them and shrinks again afterwards. The plant does not hire buses for a month and pay for them for a year.

The road itself

These routes run along a highway shared with bulkers and trailers, through villages, past cattle, and after dark through country where lions walk. Our drivers are briefed for all of it. See Lion country.

Mine and haul-road rules

A light vehicle among dump trucks is a small thing among large ones. Vehicles we place in mines carry the flag and beacon the mine requires, keep to the light-vehicle routes, and never park in a truck’s blind spot. Drivers are inducted by the mine before they enter.

Water, in a dry country

For eight months of the year this coast gets almost no rain. Haul roads turn to dust under traffic, and dust is both a hazard and a nuisance to the villages nearby. A water tanker making its rounds is part of how a site keeps its licence to operate. See Environment.
